10317-betty-gordon-at-boarding-school-or:
Alice B. Emerson published this girls' school story in 1921, sending Betty Gordon to Shadyside School after earlier books at home. New plans, letters, and good-byes open the tale, but a lost treasure soon gives Betty and her friends a puzzle to solve. The tone is bright, clean, and full of school fun.

Parties, a nutting trip, a storm, dramatics, and a Saturday race fill term time, while a mysterious four and a secret keep the plot moving. Bob's solution and a second mystery bring the treasure hunt to a close. Readers get a cheerful series tale of friendship, pluck, and schoolgirl adventure.
10372-bunch-grass-a-chronicle-of-life-on:
Horace Annesley Vachell published this ranch chronicle in 1913, dedicating it to his brother Arthur. Vachell, author of Brothers and The Hill, writes of cattle country through linked sketches rather than one straight plot. The tone is warm, comic, and full of local character, with ranch hands, neighbors, and beasts in every scene.

Chapters introduce Alethea-Belle, Pap Spooner, Gloriana, fifteen fat steers, a poisoned spring, and old man Bobo's Mandy. Experiments, pups, and barons fill the ranch year, with humor and hardship in turn. Readers get a lively, old-style portrait of western ranch life, with strong, plain folk.
10577-international-short-stories-french:
Francis J. Reynolds compiled this 1910 volume of French short stories, part of his International Short Stories series. Reynolds gathers masters from Balzac and Merimee to Maupassant, Zola, Hugo, and Daudet, with lesser-known writers beside them. The book serves readers who want French fiction in English, in one handy set.

A Piece of Bread, The Elixir of Life, Mateo Falcone, Zadig, Abandoned, Jean Gourdon's Four Days, and The Last Lesson stand among the pieces. Love, war, wit, and moral surprise recur. Readers get a rich, varied anthology of French storytelling, from classic tales to modern sketches.
10762-impressions-of-theophrastus-such:
George Eliot published Impressions of Theophrastus Such in 1879, a book of essays spoken by an imagined observer of modern life. Its chapters look inward and backward. They take up how we encourage research, a man surprised at his own originality, a too deferential man, moral swindlers, and the shadows of the coming race. Theophrastus judges his age in the manner of his ancient namesake.

Eliot writes with irony and moral seriousness, turning small social types into lessons on honesty, vanity, and thought. The essays are short, sharp, and quotable. Readers get the great novelist as a critic of her own society, in her last published work.
10946-three-frenchmen-in-bengal-the-comm:
S. C. Hill, officer in charge of India's government records, wrote this 1903 history of French Bengal's ruin in 1757. Three chiefs carry the story: Renault at Chandernagore, Law at Cossimbazar, and Courtin at Dacca. Maps and plans show the Ganges valley, the Hugli River, and the forts where French trade centred.

Hill explains why France lost: Calcutta's English merchants traded freely across Bengal, while French traders faced restrictions and poorer sites, though Calcutta, Chandernagore, and Chinsurah stood within thirty miles of one another. War with England then destroyed the French settlements. The book uses official records to tell a sharp story of commercial rivalry, and it remains a clear account of a forgotten imperial contest.
11248-the-delights-of-wisdom-pertaining-:
Emanuel Swedenborg's Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love, put into English from the Latin work printed at Amsterdam in 1768. argues that true marriage continues in heaven, while its companion section treats the pleasures of scortatory, or illicit, love as insanity. Swedenborg opens by saying plainly that the visions he recalls, visions of angels, weddings in heaven, and spirit groups, were seen in perfect wakefulness over twenty-five years, not invented as fiction.

The book's teaching on God is ordered and odd: angels debate, companies from north and south assemble, and earthly marriage matches a heavenly pattern. Readers need not accept Swedenborg's visions to follow his argument about love, fidelity, and the afterlife. The work remains central to his school's thought and to the history of mystic writers.
11363-bayard-the-good-knight-without-fea:
Christopher Hare's Bayard, the Good Knight Without Fear and Without Reproach, with colored illustrations by Herbert Cole. retells the joyful history of Pierre Terrail, born at Bayard Castle in Dauphiné about 1474, when Louis XI ruled France. Second son of a large, heroic family, Bayard grew up in a castle built on a rocky hill in 1404, commanding a deep valley. Illustrations show his horsemanship, the battle of Fornovo, his defense of a bridge, and his death.

Hare writes for young readers, presenting Bayard as chivalry's model: brave, loyal, and courteous. The book's old-fashioned title promises exactly what it delivers, a life of heroic deeds. For readers of historical biography for children, it remains a charming introduction to late medieval France.
1206-the-flying-u-ranch:
B. M. Bower returns to the Flying U ranch in Montana, where the Happy Family of cowboys, led by Chip Bennett, rides, jokes, and brawls through a season of work and trouble. A new foreman, a schoolteacher, and a nest of rustlers stir the crew, and the ranch's fortunes hang on wit and nerve.

Bower writes cowboy life with humor and affection, and her dialogue crackles with range talk. The novel is episodic and warm, more about a crew than a single hero. It gives a lively picture of the working West and still pleases western fans.
12486-indian-nullification-of-the-uncons:
William Apes, an Indian and preacher of the gospel, published this 1835 defence of the Mashpee tribe against Massachusetts law. Apes addresses the white people of Massachusetts directly, calling them descendants of men who crossed the sea to escape tyranny, and asking why that refuge now denies Indians self-rule.

The pamphlet explains the pretended riot at Mashpee, arguing that tribal resistance to state laws was lawful nullification, not disorder. Apes sets tribal rights, Christian preaching and American principle side by side. The tract stands as an early Native American political text, written by a Mashpee advocate in his own voice, and it remains a sharp record of the Mashpee struggle.
12629-language-an-introduction-to-the-st:
Edward Sapir's Language, an Introduction to the Study of Speech, first published in 1921 and reprinted in 1939, defines language as a cultural, not biologically inherited, function. Sapir dismisses interjectional and sound-imitative theories of origin as futile, and builds a definition on the psycho-physical basis of speech.

Chapters move from elements of speech and sounds of language through forms, grammar and types of linguistic structure. Words, sentences, feeling-tones, concepts and thought without language all receive treatment. Sapir writes with clarity for general readers, and the book remains a classic introduction to linguistics, humane and systematic.
12769-how-to-teach:
George Drayton Strayer and Naomi Norsworthy published How to Teach in 1917 as a practical guide for classroom teachers. It treats education as a group enterprise, aimed at making pupils active for the common good, not merely polished as individuals. Chapters cover attention, habit, memory, imagination, play, moral conduct, and study methods.

Later sections weigh verbal images against object images, arguing that words save time and travel further, while concrete images ground creative work and hard thinking. Tests and measures of children's progress close the book. Teachers will find here the psychology of its day turned into plain classroom counsel.
13084-back-to-methuselah-a-metabiologica:
Bernard Shaw's 1921 Back to Methuselah, subtitled a metabiological pentateuch, is a five-part play cycle on evolution, long life, and the future of man. Its long preface moves from Darwin and the neo-Darwinians to creative evolution, voluntary longevity, and the hope, or lack of it, in education. Shaw argues that life strives upward by will, not by blind chance alone.

The plays range from Eden to a far future where men live for centuries and debate whether to kill, drink, or wait for tomorrow. One scene hears Beethoven's Hammerklavier as a picture of whirling electrons, sane and methodical beneath its difficulty. Shaw's cycle is bold, talkative, and comic, a philosopher's drama dressed as science fiction.
13482-what-the-schools-teach-and-might-t:
Franklin Bobbitt, of the University of Chicago, reports what Cleveland schools teach and might teach in this 1915 survey volume, directed by Leonard P. Ayres for the Cleveland Foundation. Tables measure time given to reading, spelling, handwriting, language, composition, and grammar, with sets of supplementary books per building.

Bobbitt argues that spelling for the few who need it unusually well should not be forced on all. Spelling practice should run through high school, with teachers refusing written work full of errors. Drawing, taught in measured hours across grades, gets its own tables. The survey is a practical audit of an American city school system, asking what each subject is worth in time and result.
14641-the-golden-calf-which-the-world-ad:
John Frederick Helvetius, doctor at The Hague, wrote The Golden Calf in Latin in 1666, and this English version, printed in London in 1670, tells how lead was transmuted into gold. The title names the world's adored metal.

A grave stranger in plebeian habit visits Helvetius, asks leave to discuss the pyrotechnic art, and demonstrates the philosopher's stone in a tiny particle. Helvetius dedicates the work to physicians of Amsterdam and Brandenburg. The book is a famous alchemical testimony, credulous to modern eyes but central to the history of chemistry's dreams. Alchemists cited Helvetius for generations after.
15429-thomas-henry-huxley-a-character-sk:
Leonard Huxley wrote this short life of his father, Thomas Henry Huxley, for the Rationalist Press Association in 1920. It is a character sketch rather than a full biography, tracing a scientist who became a public voice for science in Victorian Britain. Portraits from youth to old age illustrate the text.

Chapters follow Huxley's medical training, his voyage on the Rattlesnake, and his long fight for Darwin's Origin of Species in lecture halls and print. Later sections cover his work for popular education, for teachers and women students, and his views on ethics and the Church. Family scenes and letters close the book, showing the private man behind the debater. It suits readers who want a compact, humane portrait of a famous Victorian mind.
1697-madam-how-and-lady-why-or-first-les:
Charles Kingsley wrote this book of talks for children, in which a father answers his son's questions about the world outdoors by telling stories of Madam How and Lady Why. Madam How stands for the forces that shape the earth — water, ice, fire, and weather — while Lady Why stands for the reasons behind what those forces do.

Chapters take the reader to seashores, chalk cliffs, volcanoes, and coral reefs. Each walk ends with a plain account of how a valley was cut or a rock was laid down. It is an early work of popular science for the young, meant to be read aloud, and it still works as a friendly first step into geology.
1720-the-man-who-knew-too-much:
Gilbert K. Chesterton links eight detective stories around Horne Fisher, a man who knows too much about the powerful and too little about how to use what he knows. A face in a target, a prince who vanishes, a schoolboy's soul, and a temple of silence each hide a crime that polite society would rather not name.

Fisher solves his cases by seeing the political motive behind the puzzle, and Chesterton uses each mystery to poke at privilege, war, and the press. The stories are witty and compact, and they reward readers who like their detection mixed with argument about how England is really run.
1902-the-old-peabody-pew-a-christmas-rom:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Old Peabody Pew, a Christmas romance of a country church, is dedicated to a handful of dear New England women. Their names are unknown to the world, and they dwell in a quiet village. They worked together to make their corner of the universe pleasanter. The story follows those women as they prepare the church for Christmas.

Household work done and luncheons laid out for the men of the family, the women turn to the pew itself, and to the old romance it holds. Wiggin writes the tale with warmth and a light touch. Its charm lies in its setting: a village church at Christmas, and the love story that its oldest pew remembers.
20055-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote Historic Tales, a set of books that retell great events as stories. Volume six turns to France, under the subtitle The Romance of Reality. One scene opens on a grand plain in the centre of France. There stands an old, rich city that stood before France itself began.

Morris moves from Rome's wide rule to later French history in vivid scenes. He aimed to make the past read like a tale, not a list. Readers get battles, kings, and cities told in a flowing style. The volume suits those who learn history best through story.
2086-the-slowcoach:
E. V. Lucas writes a children's story about the Avory family of Chiswick, whose mother and four children take to the road in a caravan called the Slowcoach. Janet, Robert, Hester, and little Gregory Bruce travel with high spirits. Lucas wrote the book for children who loved caravans, camps, and the open road.

Adventures follow at every stop: a second caravan, a runaway pony, a lost baby, a giant, and a visit to Stratford-on-Avon. Lucas keeps the tone kind and funny, and the book charms as a gentle road tale for young readers. Stratford-on-Avon gives the journey a literary stop, since Shakespeare's town draws every traveller.
2099-a-history-of-the-moravian-church:
J. E. Hutton writes a full history of the Moravian Church, from the Bohemian Brethren of 1457 through Hus, Peter of Chelcic, and the society at Kunwald to the modern church. The second edition of 1909 revises and enlarges the work. Hutton revised and enlarged the history for its second edition in 1909.

Hutton follows the Brethren through persecution, exile, and renewal, with chapters on Poland, missions, and church order. The history suits readers who want a clear, detailed account of one of Protestantism's oldest communities. The Moravians, heirs of the Bohemian Brethren, spread missions from Herrnhut across the world.
21035-the-adventures-of-a-three-guinea-w:
A watch scarce a month old settles to business at once, Talbot Baines Reed observes. Watches, he jokes, outgrow infancy far faster than human babes ever do. The Adventures of a Three Guinea Watch lets that watch tell its own tale.

From pocket to pocket, the watch sees school, city, wealth, and want at close range. Owners come and go while its small voice judges them all with wit. Reed's device lets him tour all ranks of life in one tale. The book charms as both school story and social sketch, ticked out in a watch's own dry time.
21068-under-the-meteor-flag-log-of-a-mid:
On March 9, 1793, the gun-brig Scourge sailed from Spithead to cruise for a month in the Channel. A young midshipman kept the log in Harry Collingwood's novel. Britain was entering the French Revolutionary War. The boy narrator serves under orders to watch for enemy activity close to home.

Gales, shipwrecks, rafts, and hand-to-hand fights fill his service, in the manner of the boys' sea tales of Kingston. The young midshipman proves smarter and luckier than his years suggest. One odd note is the title: the meteor flag appears only once, at a burial at sea.
21346-the-sot-weed-factor-or-a-voyage-to:
Ebenezer Cooke published this satire in London in 1708, a burlesque poem about a tobacco factor's voyage to Maryland. Sot-weed is tobacco, the colony's money crop, and its factor its often-duped agent. The title page promises the laws, courts, buildings, feasts, and drunken humours of the inhabitants of that part of America.

Cooke's newcomer finds courts, food, drink, and manners all turned upside down for an English gentleman. Shea's Early Southern Tracts reprinted the poem in the nineteenth century, noting how personal and earnest its mockery feels. It is among the earliest comic poems written about America, and still one of the sharpest colonial satires.
21471-mountain-moggy-the-stoning-of-the-:
Old Mountain Moggy lives alone on a Welsh hillside in W. H. G. Kingston's short tale Mountain Moggy. Local children call her a witch who can never be hurt or die. They amuse themselves by taunting her and throwing stones at her hut.

One evening a stone knocks a burning stick from her fire, and the flames catch her. A young midshipman, lost nearby, helps her and brings word to the village. The clergyman, once a doctor, hurries up to treat her wounds. Moggy's pardon of William, a ringleader in the stoning, gives the tale its theme of forgiveness.
22534-a-biographical-sketch-of-the-life-:
A Biographical Sketch of the Life and Character of Joseph Ch. preserves a grandfather's memory for his descendants. The writer addresses beloved children directly in its opening lines. Your grandfather, he tells them, was a truly great man.

Not as a warrior, the sketch insists, nor as a statesman. His greatness was not of the earth, earthy kind at all. He possessed a rare combination of moral worth and Christian excellence. That made him a blessing to his race and family. In other words, he was great because he was truly good. Such family memorials kept private virtues in public print. Readers get Victorian praise of character over fame or wealth.
22578-the-girl-and-the-kingdom-learning-:
The Girl and the Kingdom, subtitled Learning to Teach, is a work of fiction about a young woman finding her calling as a teacher in a crowded city neighborhood. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its setting is a poor immigrant district where shop signs carry names from many nations.

The sample pages describe tailors and secondhand shops run by Jewish families alongside liquor sellers with Irish and Scottish names. Against that lively street scene, the story follows its heroine's path into teaching. Readers get both a character story and a close look at city teaching in an era of heavy immigration. The book speaks to readers drawn to education, social work, and urban life of the period.
23054-the-dean-s-watch:
Erckmann-Chatrian waylay a traveler in The Dean's Watch, their tale dated 1897 in this edition. A stranger hails traveling musicians on the Heidelberg road, guessing their errand, and presses advice on them. Wilfred studies him sidelong and answers shortly, asking what business it could possibly be of his. The stranger's counsel comes free all the same, and entirely unasked.

The Alsatian writing pair built their fame on village tales where small objects carry long histories. A dean's watch, ticking through the story, measures out guilt, memory, and time itself. Their manner is plain and patient, letting dread accumulate in ordinary rooms. This translation brought their Rhineland world to English readers who prized its solidity.
23227-aucassin-and-nicolette-translated-:
Aucassin and Nicolette is an old French tale, presented here in a translation by Francis William Bourdillon. Its young hero, Aucassin, is pressed hard by both his parents. They urge him to take up his arms, mount his horse, fight for his land, and stand by his father's men.

If his men see him in their midst, his parents promise, they will fight harder for their lives, their goods, and his land. That pressure sets the tale's core tension: duty in war against the pull of love. Readers get one of medieval France's best-loved short tales in plain English dress.
2993-samuel-butler-a-sketch:
Henry Festing Jones wrote Samuel Butler: A Sketch, first published in The Humour of Homer and Other Essays in 1913 and reissued by Jonathan Cape in 1921. Butler was born on December 4, 1835, at the rectory in Langar, Nottinghamshire, son of the Reverend Thomas Butler, later a canon of Lincoln Cathedral, and Fanny Worsley of Bristol. His grandfather was Dr. Samuel Butler, the famous headmaster.

Jones follows Butler as artist as well as author, noting a dozen pictures exhibited at the Royal Academy between 1868 and 1876, including Mr. Heatherley's Holiday, hung on the line in 1874. Butler left the painting to his college friend Jason Smith, whose representatives gave it to the nation. The sketch gives a compact life of a singular Victorian thinker.
3632-poor-miss-finch:
Wilkie Collins writes a sensation novel about a blind heroine, Lucilla Finch, called Poor Miss Finch. Collins notes in his dedication that many charming blind girls had appeared in fiction and drama before, but almost always from an ideal and sentimental point of view. His attempt, he says, is to appeal to a different interest: blindness as lived, with its practical limits and its sharp senses.

The story mixes romance, mystery, and a villain's plot around Lucilla, whose blindness makes her both vulnerable and keenly observant. Collins keeps the suspense moving while treating his heroine with respect. The novel suits readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction and a heroine who sees more than sighted people expect.
3724-the-house-of-heine-brothers-in-muni:
Anthony Trollope sets this tale in the dingy Munich office of Heine Brothers, bankers of good repute but modest scale. The two elderly brothers sit daily in the Schrannen Platz, and the younger handles any business that needs more than a word or two. Into their quiet world comes Herbert Onslow, a young Englishman in love with their daughter Isa, and the tale turns on whether prudence will let the match proceed.

Isa has promised her mother that nothing shall change between the pair in manner, since they are not betrothed and may never be. Herbert frets and fumes at the delay, while daily meetings keep hope alive. The story is a gentle study of family caution against young love, with a Bavarian banking house as its unlikely stage.
4000-the-immortals-masterpieces-of-ficti:
Georges Ohnet's volume belongs to the French Immortals series of fiction crowned by the French Academy, and it gathers prize-winning short tales. A sampled chapter, The Little Boots, opens on worn laced boots set in a line by a door, their leather marked by the feet that wore them.

Such small, telling details carry these stories, which favor character and feeling over grand plot. Ohnet and his fellow laureates write of French homes, work, and love with warmth and care. Readers who enjoy short, humane fiction will find the volume a pleasant door into the Academy's chosen storytellers.
4001-widger-s-quotations-from-project-gu:
David Widger gathered this set of short sayings from the Project Gutenberg editions of French novels crowned by the French Academy. The lines come from many hands and many plots, yet they share a plain, sharp way of judging life.

Readers will find maxims on dignity and revenge, on love earned by desert, on self-interest as the law of the world, and on sense that looks like nonsense. Each line stands alone, so the book works well in small bites, for browsing or for copying into a commonplace book. It offers a quick taste of the wit and moral bite of the French Immortals series.
4020-arcadian-adventures-with-the-idle-r:
A comic novel of New York's idle rich follows the members of a plutocratic club through dinners, lectures, and college follies. Notices in a college hall tell of classes suspended and professors struck down by overwork, while bronze busts watch from niches.

The humor turns on wealth without work, as rich men take up causes, cures, and learning with grand seriousness and small sense. The book satirizes a gilded world of clubs, yachts, and good intentions gone idle. Readers who enjoy light social satire will find a funny, old-fashioned portrait of money at play.
4377-mrs-wiggs-of-the-cabbage-patch:
Alice Caldwell Hegan wrote this little story of Mrs. Wiggs, first published in 1901 and dedicated to her mother, the good angel of the Cabbage Patch. The Cabbage Patch is a poor Louisville neighborhood, and Mrs. Wiggs meets its cold mornings with cheer, even when her elbows stick through a boy's coat. Her philosophy opens the book.

Later chapters bring ways and means, the Christmas lady, the annexation of Cuby, a theater party, and Mr. Bob. Mrs. Wiggs at home, spring in the patch, and a benefit dance complete the picture. Hegan's tale is warm and funny, and it made Mrs. Wiggs a beloved figure of American humor.
4760-tillie-a-mennonite-maid-a-story-of-:
Helen Reimensnyder Martin tells Tillie, a Mennonite Maid, as a story of the Pennsylvania Dutch. Its chapters open with Tillie crying, Oh, I love her, and with a teacher promising, I'm going to learn you once. Later chapters ask what is hurting Tillie, show the Doc combining business and pleasure, and declare that novels are not moral, Doc. Jake Getz falls into a quandary, and the last days of Pump-Eye pass.

Miss Margaret runs an errand, Tillie promises to do her darn best, teacher, and Adam Schunk's funeral follows. Tillie feels plain, Absalom keeps company, Ezra Herr the pedagogue appears, and a Harvard graduate arrives. The Wackernagels at home, Tillie revealing herself, telling a lie, and being set back lead to a revolt of Tillie and a last fight. Readers get a warm, dialect-rich novel of a bright girl among strict Mennonite ways.
4983-slips-of-speech:
John H. Bechtel's Slips of Speech opens with taste as a universal gift, found in some degree in all nations and ages, from the savage's love of decoration to civilized man's love of art. Taste differs among people as faces and languages differ, and the same person shows it differently at different periods of life.

That variety, Bechtel argues, implies a susceptibility to improvement, and good taste in writing is no exception. The book collects common errors and lapses in speech and writing, correcting them with examples. Readers who want cleaner English get a practical guide, written before style books became standard, and still useful for its plain advice.
6818-the-arctic-prairies-a-canoe-journey:
Ernest Thompson Seton, author of Wild Animals I Have Known, canoes two thousand miles in search of caribou, north of Aylmer Lake, in The Arctic Prairies. Seton dedicates the book to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, premier of Canada. It opens with a wish. What young man would not give a year to roll back time five decades? He could live in the romantic Wild West. Buffalo would pasture by the Missouri, and traders would swap news by horse and canoe, months apart.

Seton's own voyage, by canoe through northern lakes and prairies, seeks the caribou herds in a land still wild. His prose mixes naturalist care with adventure. The Arctic Prairies is a classic, stirring account of a northern journey, full of wildlife and wonder.
6857-indian-games-an-historical-research:
Andrew McFarland Davis studies Indian games as history, opening with Father Brebeuf's 1636 note on the Hurons. Three games were in vogue, Brebeuf says: cross, platter, and straw, the first two deemed supreme for health. A sick man, hot with fever and foreseeing death, might be ordered a game of cross as his only cooling remedy, or might dream he must die unless his country plays.

Davis traces those games, their rules, meanings, and rites, with scholarly care. His work shows play as medicine, ritual, and social bond. Indian Games is a learned, early study of Native play, valuable to readers of anthropology and history.
7007-the-true-story-of-my-life-a-sketch:
Hans Christian Andersen's true story of his life appears here in Mary Howitt's translation, sent to Munroe and Company as proof sheets of an unpublished life. Howitt notes this is the author's edition, with Andersen sharing in the proceeds, and she dates her letter from London on June 29, 1847. The English translation is inscribed to Jenny Lind, in admiration of her beautiful talents and still more beautiful life.

An editor's note warns many words lack letters, since diacritic marks were missing from the digital file's character set at production. The sketch itself tells Andersen's rise from poor beginnings to fame, in his own voice as Howitt renders it. It remains a short, direct autobiography from the storyteller himself.
7021-indian-frontier-policy-an-historica:
General Sir John Adye sketches Indian frontier policy on the North West frontier, with a map, at a time of large military operations against a combination of independent tribes. He warns the present troubles are no sudden outbreak by turbulent neighbors, since their causes lie far deeper in events of bygone years. His short historical summary traces the varying phases of policy, hoping to help the public grasp its general bearings.

Adye writes for readers who must form a correct opinion of the policy to pursue in future, not merely follow the news of a campaign. The sketch weighs Britain's Eastern Empire, tribal independence, and the cost of force against patience. It is a soldier's brief for understanding before judgment on the frontier.
712-thomas-jefferson-a-character-sketch:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this sketch of Thomas Jefferson for a series on great Americans, with a supplementary essay by G. Mercer Adam. It traces Jefferson from birth and youth to the presidency, stressing his learning, his democratic faith, and his role in shaping the young republic. An account of the Louisiana Purchase and a set of anecdotes and dates round out the portrait.

Ellis paints Jefferson as wise, prudent, and deeply patriotic, a man who saw both the promise and the perils of the new nation. The sketch is laudatory, as such popular lives often were, yet it gathers the key facts of his career in short compass. It serves as a friendly first life of the third president for general readers.
7125-catherine-booth-a-sketch:
Colonel Mildred Duff sketches Catherine Booth, reprinted from The Warriors Library, with a preface by General Bramwell Booth. Duff penned this warm and moving portrait of his mother at Bramwell Booth's urging, hoping readers might walk the same faithful path she did. Booth answers the doubt: was not Missus Booth exceptional, gifted, and specially trained, so how can ordinary people follow her.

Let me tell you, he replies: Missus Booth walked with God. As a shy young girl lending her mother a hand at home, she kept reaching toward God. Years later, famous across many countries, praised in print, and cherished by good people everywhere, she lived exactly as before. The sketch that follows traces that steady faith.
7496-jack-ranger-s-western-trip-or-from-:
Clarence Young's Jack Ranger series begins at Washington Hall, the boarding school of Dr. Henry Mead on Rudmore Lake, sometimes called Lakeside Academy. The crowd of boys starts forth on mischief bent. The early chapters are schoolboy comedy: fun at Washington Hall, Jack in trouble, a threatening letter, a lesson in chemistry, and a burglary scare foiled by quick wits.

Then comes Nat's invitation, and ho for the West. The second half moves to ranch and range: an old acquaintance, a professor's trick, shooting an oil well, a wild steer, an old stockman, and a thief in the night. Jack hears news of his father as the trail leads toward finding Orion Tevis. The book is a sturdy boys' adventure, half school story and half western.
7819-an-enquiry-into-an-origin-of-honour:
Bernard Mandeville, author of The Fable of the Bees, asks in An Enquiry into the Origin of Honour whether honor and virtue come from God or from human invention. His preface defends an earlier essay on moral virtue against charges of crime, and asks readers to hear his case with patience.

Mandeville holds that even heathen virtue was made by men, not heaven. Through dialogues on morals, manners, and war, he probes how pride, praise, and faith shape soldiers and citizens. It is a sharp, early work of moral philosophy, still keen on how praise steers conduct.
8198-the-fourth-watch:
H. A. Cody, author of The Frontiersman and The Long Patrol, wrote The Fourth Watch for messengers, watchmen. And stewards of the Lord who have toiled through life's long night and now, in their fourth and last watch, behold a new life breaking. Dedicated by one still in the second watch, the novel's chapters move from an awakening and a vision, through Glendow Rectory. The warder of the night, the breath of slander, and an auction, to the Farringtons, the golden key, and guarding the flock.

Cody, a Canadian clergyman-novelist, writes a story of ministry, village life, and faith under trial. The night-watch image gives the book its structure and its comfort: darkness is long, but dawn comes. For readers of religious fiction, it is a earnest, old-fashioned novel of pastoral life and perseverance.
8425-caesar-a-sketch:
James Anthony Froude calls this work a sketch because, as his preface says, the materials do not exist for a portrait of Julius Caesar at once authentic and complete. The original authorities are thin, and Froude works from what survives to outline Caesar's life, character, and times, quoting Shakespeare's Henry V as his apology for daring so great an object.

Froude, the Victorian historian, writes with narrative force, and his Caesar is a statesman of genius in a republic falling apart. Readers get a readable, opinionated life, more sketch than scholarly biography, and a view of how Victorians judged Rome's fall. It pairs well with fuller modern lives, as a period portrait.
8433-the-vagabond-and-other-poems-from-p:
R. C. Lehmann gathers poems that first appeared in Punch, the London humorous weekly, with all but two pieces drawn from its pages. Published in 1918 by John Lane, the volume shows Lehmann, author of Anni Fugaces and Light and Shade, in his lightest vein: verses for a magazine audience, urbane, witty, and topical.

Punch verse was meant to amuse educated readers over breakfast, and Lehmann's pieces do that work with polish. The vagabond of the title sets the tone, a wanderer through modern life with a smile. Readers of light verse will find a period piece, charming and slight, and a reminder of how widely Punch once set the tone of English humor.
8574-racketty-packetty-house-as-told-by-:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells this children's story through Queen Crosspatch, ruler of the doll world, who insists dolls get up to plenty when no one is watching. When backs are turned, they dance, sing, play the piano, and enjoy themselves; the moment someone looks, they freeze. The tale contrasts two doll families: one tidy and well liked, the other noisy and neglected.

Harrison Cady's pictures match the playful tone, and the story stays close to a child's logic about toys having secret lives. Burnett, already famous for Little Lord Fauntleroy, keeps the sentences simple and the humour gentle. Young readers get a short, funny fable about fairness and manners, while older readers can enjoy it as a small classic of nursery storytelling.
9454-orchesography-or-the-art-of-dancing:
John Weaver, a London dancing master, published Orchesography in 1706, a guide to the art of dance notation. It translates the French system of Monsieur Feuillet into English, with signs and figures for steps. Weaver claims any dancer who knows the craft can learn new dances from the page alone. The book also gives rules for the motions of the arms.

Tables set out all steps used in dancing, so a reader can read a dance as one reads music. The text notes that the work leans on diagrams, which is why this file holds no full text version. A reader gets a rare window on Baroque dance craft, and on how an age first tried to write motion down in print.
9479-the-boy-life-of-napoleon-afterwards:
Madame Eugénie Foa, a beloved French writer for children, wrote the boy life of Napoleon, here adapted for American boys and girls in 1895. Foa, famed for forty years in French homes, told history tales with pure tone and high morals. This book follows Napoleon from boyhood toward the throne he would one day seize. Vesper L. George drew the pictures.

Chapters trace the young Corsican's school days, pride, study, and early trials, with drama fit for young readers. Foa stresses truth to history as well as lively action. A reader gets a warm, old-style life of a great captain's youth, and a glimpse of how French children once learned their hero's tale.
9796-the-master-detective-being-some-fur:
Percy James Brebner wrote The Master Detective in 1916, further cases of Christopher Quarles, his consulting sleuth. Contents list the strange case of Sir Grenville Rusholm, the kidnapping of Eva Wilkison, and the Delverton affair. A house in Manleigh Road, a stolen aeroplane model, and a contessa's pearls follow. The crime in a yellow taxi and a jeweled chalice add color.

Quarles opens with Rusholm dead, blinds down, and obituaries in every paper. Each case tests his quiet reason against bold crime. A reader gets a classic Edwardian detective set, brisk and ingenious, with a sleuth of the Holmes school.
9957-the-personal-touch:
J. Wilbur Chapman, an American evangelist, wrote this book on personal Christian work, opening with his own testimony. He argues that faith spreads best not by crowds alone but by one person speaking plainly to another, and he states the general principle behind that claim.

Chapters offer a polished shaft, starting right, winning the young, and winning and holding converts, with practical illustrations and a final word on conversion as a miracle. Chapman's tone is direct and pastoral. Readers interested in evangelism a century ago will find its methods and motives set out clearly.
a-history-of-the-moravian-church:
J. E. Hutton writes a full history of the Moravian Church in this second edition, revised and enlarged, dated 1909 on its title page. Book one, The Bohemian Brethren, runs from 1457 to 1673 and opens with the rising storm in Bohemia and the burning of Hus in 1415. Persecuted brethren organize at Kunwald under Gregory the Patriarch.

Later books follow Luke of Prague, John Augusta's sufferings, the Brethren in Poland and exile, then Count Zinzendorf, the founding of Herrnhut, and the church's worldwide missions. Hutton writes as a sympathetic insider with a historian's care for dates and documents. The book remains a standard one-volume account of a small church with a vast missionary reach.
arcadian-adventures-with-the-idle-rich:
Stephen Leacock's Arcadian Adventures with the Idle Rich, his 1914 satire of a North American city's millionaires, opens at the Mausoleum Club on Plutoria Avenue. Infants in perambulators own distilleries and railway mergers while their fathers lunch downtown. The eight linked sketches follow Mr. Lucullus Fyshe's little dinner and the wizardry of finance that rules the avenue. Mrs. Rasselyer-Brown's oriental society and Mr. Tomlinson's arrested philanthropy come next in the contents.

Inside, the rival churches of St. Asaph and St. Osoph compete like department stores for rich souls. The Reverend Uttermust Dumfarthing ministers to congregations who prefer their gospel comfortable. A great fight for clean government ends, as Leacock's fights do, with the reformers absorbed by the machine. Readers get the Canadian humorist at his most surgical: a city where money has replaced every other faith, described in prose so smooth the victims would enjoy it.
aubin-histoire-diables-loudun-1694-frenc:
Nicolas Aubin published his Histoire des Diables de Loudun in French in 1694. Loudun was the town in France where Ursuline nuns claimed to be possessed in the 1630s. Aubin built his account from the first records of the case, close to sixty years after the events.

At the center stands Urbain Grandier, the priest accused of causing the possessions by sorcery. Grandier was tried and put to death in 1634, and Aubin follows that grim story step by step. The book became the base account of the most famous possession case of its century. Later writers on Loudun still lean on it.
bavent-histoire-madeleine-bavent-1652-fr:
Madeleine Bavent was a nun at Louviers, in France, during the possessions said to grip her convent from 1642 to 1647. Her own story, told in the first person, was printed in French in 1652. The text here follows the 1878 reprint, which adds a life of Bavent and extra papers.

Bavent tells what she said she saw, feared, and confessed while priests and judges pressed the case. The added papers include her arrest and the formal record of her words. Few possession cases left so direct a voice from the accused woman herself. That closeness makes the book a key source on Louviers.
catherine-booth-a-sketch:
Mildred Duff's Catherine Booth: A Sketch, reprinted from The Warriors' Library, tells the life of the Salvation Army's co-founder. General Bramwell Booth, her son, supplies a preface, praising Duff's interesting and touching account of his dear mother.

Bramwell Booth answers the natural question: was Mrs. Booth not exceptional, with great gifts and special training? He replies that she walked with God, from her days as a timid girl helping her mother at home to her fame among multitudes. Readers interested in the Salvation Army, or in Victorian women preachers, will find Duff's sketch short, affectionate and inspiring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-echt:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Echternach describes a Benedictine house in Luxemburg, founded in 698 by St. Willibrord. Willibrord, an English monk of Ripon, was apostle of Friesland and first bishop of Utrecht. He ruled the house as abbot until his death in 739, on land given by St. Irmine, Abbess of Oeren.

Kings, including Pepin and Charlemagne, heaped gifts on Echternach. After secular canons displaced the monks in 859, Emperor Otto the First brought back Benedictine life in 971 with forty monks from St. Maximin at Trier. The house became one of northern Europe's most famed, flourishing until the French Revolution closed it and scattered its monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achimelech:
Achimelech is a name borne by several men in scripture, and this entry separates them. First is the priest of Nobe who sheltered David during his flight from Saul. For that hospitality he was put to death with all the priests of Nobe, except his son Abiathar, who escaped and joined David. Second is a Hethite companion of the outlawed David.

Third is an Achimelech called son of Abiathar and associate of Sadoc in the priesthood, though that post is usually given to Abiathar, son of Achimelech. The entry judges the son of Abiathar reading an accidental transposition in Kings that also affected Paralipomenon. Fourth, Psalm 33's title gives Achis, King of Geth, the name Achimelech, where some texts read Abimelech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-and-pe:
Adrian and Peter von Walenburch were Cologne auxiliary bishops and celebrated controversial theologians, born at Rotterdam early in the seventeenth century, with exact birth dates unknown. Adrian died at Mainz or Wiesbaden in September 1669, and Peter died at Cologne in December 1675. Early accounts disagree over whether the brothers were Protestants or Catholics in youth.

They studied law in France and took doctorates in civil and canon law, then studied Catholic theology after returning to Rotterdam. Religious turmoil in Holland drove them to Germany, and in 1647 Cologne's archbishop made Adrian auxiliary bishop and vicar-general. Peter became canon at Mainz, titular Bishop of Mysia in 1658, and later auxiliary bishop of Cologne. Peter aided Leibniz's theological studies for church reunion, and their Tractatus de controversiis fidei of 1671 holds seventeen treatises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aldersbach:
Aldersbach was once a Cistercian abbey in Lower Bavaria's Vils valley. St. Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, founded it in 1127, first as a house of canons regular. In 1146 his successor Egilbert gave the foundation to the Cistercians, with Abbot Sefried and monks from Ebrach taking possession. Under Cistercian rule the abbey flourished, kept strict discipline, and sent out daughter houses at Fürstenfeld, Fürstenzell, and Gotteszell.

The monks farmed the soil, served neighbouring churches, and pursued learning. The first abbot founded a library that later abbots enlarged, and monks studied at Paris, Vienna, Padua, Heidelberg, and Ingolstadt. War ravaged the house, above all in the Thirty Years' War, when it was pillaged and nearly abandoned, though the library survived. Suppressed on 1 April 1803 with forty monks, its church became a parish church and its library passed to the National Library at Munich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambo-in-the-r:
The ambo has practically disappeared from the Roman Rite, its only reminder the pulpit or reading desk. Two ambos sometimes served, one for Epistle and one for Gospel, as at Rome's St. Clement and Venice's St. Mark. In the Russian Orthodox Church the ambo now means two or three semicircular steps from the soleas to the floor, directly before the royal doors.

Russian cathedrals add another mid-nave ambo, where the bishop stands during parts of the pontifical service. Greek Orthodox usage keeps the ambo's ancient style, though moved from middle to sides. The closing prayer behind the ambo is said before the royal doors outside the iconostasis. In the Greek Catholic Church, Slavic and American, the ambo is a table before the royal doors holding crucifix and two candles. Baptisms, confirmations, and marriages are performed there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amorbach:
A Benedictine abbey in Lower Franconia, Bavaria, stands about twenty-five miles south of Aschaffenburg. The town that grew around its walls shares its name. Saint Pirmin founded the house early in the eighth century. Count Ruthard had called him to preach in the region, and the abbey church was consecrated in 734.

Its monks carried Christianity through the Oden forest and into northern Germany. There they helped convert the Saxons, and several early bishops of Verden had served as abbots here. Gifts from Charles Martel and his sons enriched the house. Yet Huns, Peasants' War fighters, and Swedish troops each damaged it in turn. Rebuilt in the seventeenth century, with a church long famed for its organ, the abbey was suppressed in 1803 and passed to Bavaria in 1816.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Norwich took its present name only in the eleventh century. Its history runs five hundred years further back, to the conversion of East Anglia by Saint Felix in the reign of King Sigeberht. Felix fixed his see at Dunwich, a coastal town since swallowed by the sea in Southwold Bay, and from there he preached across Norfolk, Suffolk, and Cambridgeshire.

Thomas followed him in 647, then Beorhtgils, then Bisi. On Bisi's death in 673 Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury split the see in two, with cathedrals at Dunwich and Elmham. The article lists both successions in full, with dates where research allows. Elmham came to an end about 870, with the murder of King Edmund of the East Angles and Bishop Hunbeorht. The Dunwich line ran on toward the later Norwich see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antioch:
Antioch of Syria: modern Antakieh holds the once famous Queen of the East. With over half a million people, beautiful site, trade, culture, and military position, it rivalled Alexandria, the empire's second city. Founded in 300 B.C. by Seleucus I, Antioch stood on the Orontes, at the Lebanon and Taurus ranges' junction. Its harbour, fifteen miles distant, was Seleucia.

Unknown disciples, dispersed by Stephen's persecution, brought Christianity to Antioch. There the new Faith was preached to Greeks with such success that Christianity received its name here, perhaps as a nickname by witty Antiochenes. Acknowledged by Jerusalem's mother-church, the new community soon showed vitality and faith intelligence by spontaneous generosity to Jerusalem's brethren. Antioch, the Apostle of the Gentiles' apprenticeship place, became headquarters of Paul and Barnabas, first together, later Paul alone. Starting thence on Apostolic journeys, they brought back their work's report.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphon-in-t:
In the Greek Church, the antiphon goes back to Saint Ignatius of Antioch, third from Saint Peter in that see. Socrates says Ignatius saw angels singing the Trinity's praises in alternating hymns and gave that singing to Antioch, whence it spread to all other Churches. The Greek Church made it an integral part of Mass and of morning and evening services. It is best known as a Greek Mass portion, in first, second, and third antiphons.

While the choir sings the antiphons' versicles in turn, the priest quietly says each antiphon's prayer. These antiphons come early in Mass, after the opening Great Synapte litany, and change with the feast celebrated. Usually they have three versicles and three responses, each closing with Glory be to the Father and As it is now. The Greek Horologion, an Office book like the Roman Breviary, gives the antiphons for the year's feast-days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-ulrich:
Anton Ulrich, duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel, was born in 1633 and ruled as the most scholarly prince of his age. With his brother he became co-regent in 1685 and sole ruler in 1704. A pioneer of the German historical romance, he also wrote plays and hymns, yet his deepest study was the Fathers and the differences between Catholics and Lutherans.

He entered the Catholic Church secretly in 1710 and soon declared his conversion in public, publishing a learned apology called Fifty Motives. The book was suppressed and became rare, but his sons later secured free Catholic worship in his state. Two of his daughters followed him into the church, and the entry presents a prince whose faith cost him standing and won him a cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arch:
An arch is a structure of separate pieces, such as stone or brick, shaped as truncated wedges. They are set on a curved line so that mutual pressure holds them in place. This arcuated method contrasts with the trabeated style of Greek architecture, where lintels, or horizontal beams, spanned gaps between columns or between column and wall. The stones forming the arch's curve are called voussoirs, or arch stones, with the lowest being springers, whose joints are usually horizontal.

The upper face of the springer, where the first true arch stone starts, is skewbacked. The topmost central stone is the keystone. The concave underside is the intrados or soffit, and the convex upper side is the extrados. Piers and abutments give the arch its resting and resisting points. The entry is a builder's lexicon, defining each part before moving to arch forms and uses in church building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auch:
Auch, anciently Augusta Auscorum, is an archdiocese covering the Gers department in France. Before the Revolution it held ten suffragan sees, small bishoprics under its care, including Dax, Aire, Lectoure, and Tarbes, most of which were later merged elsewhere. Its archbishops bore the title of Aquitaine until 1789, long after any Aquitaine had ceased to exist. Re-established in 1882, the archdiocese joined the old see with Lectoure, Condom, and Lombez.

Local tradition holds that Taurinus, fifth Bishop of Eauze, moved his see to Auch. Vandals had destroyed his city, though Eauze likely stayed a metropolitan see until the Northmen invasions of the 800s. The first known Bishop of Auch is the poet St Orientius, of the early 400s, honored by a famous seventh-century abbey. Later landmarks include a council in 1276 defending church jurisdiction, and a provincial council in 1851 on faith, worship, and clerical study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auzias-march:
Auzias March was a Catalan poet, born in the last quarter of the fourteenth century at Valencia, who died there in 1458. He stands as the greatest lyric poet of older Catalan literature. Among foreigners he best captures Petrarch's love lyric, and Dante's work also shows in his imagery. His images rise above the troubadour verse his contemporaries still wrote.

Report calls him a famed soldier in Alfonso V's Naples expedition, though that report needs proof. He came of noble stock and seems to have married twice. His surviving poems hold ninety-three love songs, eight death songs, moral songs, a long spiritual song, and a brief demand to Lady Tecla. His love lady was Teresa Bou of Valencia, met, like Petrarch's Laura, in church on Good Friday. He sings her in life and in death. His work was twice turned into Castilian, first in 1539, and shaped Boscan, Garcilaso, and Mendoza.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baruch:
Baruch, Hebrew for blessed, was Jeremiah's disciple and the traditional author of the deutero-canonical book bearing his name. Son of Nerias and probably brother to Saraias, chamberlain to King Sedecias, he served the prophet through crisis. After Nebuchadnezzar plundered Jerusalem's temple in 599 BC, Baruch wrote Jeremiah's oracle at dictation and read it publicly at risk of his life. When King Joachim burned the first prophecies, Baruch wrote a second, enlarged edition.

He stayed true to Jeremiah's teachings despite bouts of despondence and perhaps personal ambition. He witnessed Jeremiah's purchase of ancestral land at Anathoth during the last siege and lived with him at Masphath after Jerusalem's fall. Tradition says both died in Egypt's path before Nebuchadnezzar invaded, though Baruch's own book complicates that account. Trent defined the Book of Baruch as sacred and canonical, and its Vulgate Latin follows the Greek fairly literally.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-hadewych: Blessed Hadewych, prioress of the Premonstratensian convent of Meer near Büderich, was born about 1150 and died about 1200. Hildegundis's daughter, she helped her mother found the convent about 1165, she succeeded her mother as prioress in 1183. Her brother Herman was provost of Kappenberg monastery from 1171 to 1210, and mother, daughter, and brother are all counted among the Blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarius-of-:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, born about 1170 near Cologne, was a learned Cistercian monk of the house near Bonn. He studied the Fathers, Boethius, and the Latin poets Virgil, Ovid, Seneca, and Claudian, and mastered a refined, fluent Latin style. On Abbot Gevard's advice he entered Heisterbach in 1199 and became master of novices, teaching new monks the austere Cistercian spirit and theology.

At Abbot Henry's request he wrote an abstract of his teaching, the famous Dialogue, and in 1228 he became prior, traveling with the abbot on visits through Germany and Friesland. His best known work is the Dialogue of Visions and Miracles in twelve books, which became likely the most popular book in Germany of its day. By 1238 he had listed thirty-six of his own works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-care-of-the-p:
Care of the poor by the Church treats charity as a branch of mercy rooted in love of God. The poor are those who cannot gain the means to live. Christ's command makes their care the duty of every Christian, yet the entry argues that organized cooperation works best, so church provision supplements rather than replaces private giving. Three grades of poverty, sorted by degree of need, frame the discussion.

After objects, history, and organization, the entry surveys national scenes, with sections on Canada, Great Britain and Ireland, and the United States. Reports of Catholic charities conferences and of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul anchor the modern picture, from a 1910 Washington conference to gatherings at St. Louis, Richmond, and Boston. The whole forms a reference survey of how an ancient duty took institutional shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carl-von-reis:
Carl von Reisach was a Bavarian churchman born at Roth in July 1800. He died in a Redemptorist monastery at Contamine in December 1869. After philosophy at Munich, he studied law at Heidelberg, Göttingen, and Landshut, taking a doctorate in both laws in 1821. He then turned to theology and was ordained in 1828 after study at the German College in Rome. Pius VII put him in charge of studies at the Propaganda College, bringing him close to the future Gregory XVI.

At Gregory's urging he attacked anti-church views in Germany, above all on mixed marriages, in an 1835 Mainz work as Athanasius Sincerus Philalethes. He became Bishop of Eichstätt in 1836, founding a boys' seminary in 1838 and a lyceum in 1843. Later he held Roman offices, from the Congregation of Ecclesiastical Affairs and the Propaganda to minister of education for the Papal States. In 1868 he became Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christchurch:
Christchurch, in New Zealand, centres a diocese covering Canterbury and Westland, part of Nelson, and the Chatham Islands. The French corvette Aube sailed in July 1840 for Akaroa to land settlers and claim the South Island for France. Lieutenant-Governor Hobson raced her there in the Britomart and proclaimed the island British four days before the French arrived.

The Canterbury Pilgrims landed at Lyttelton in December 1850 under the Canterbury Association, a High Church body whose scheme critics called a Puseyite invasion. Only 136 Catholics lived in all Canterbury in 1851, served by Marist fathers. Christchurch gained its first resident priest in 1860. Gold brought missions to the West Coast in 1864, and the diocese itself was erected in May 1887, with 35 churches, 16 schools, and 17 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-wol:
An entry on Christian Wolfgang Herdtrich, an Austrian Jesuit missionary to China, born at Graz in June 1625. He joined the Austrian Jesuits in October 1641, was chosen for the China mission in 1656, laboured two years on Celebes, then worked in Shanxi and Henan after 1660. In 1671 he was called to Peking as court mathematician, joining the scholarly Jesuits around the great emperor Kangxi.

Herdtrich knew Chinese language and literature deeply and helped write Confucius Sinarum Philosophus, published at Paris, the first translation and exposition to give European scholars real insight into the Chinese sage. He also wrote a large Chinese-Latin dictionary. His last nine years passed as superior of the Jiangzhou mission in Shanxi, and Kangxi himself composed his epitaph after his death in July 1684.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-of-ant:
An entry on the Church of Antioch and the city that mothered it, founded about 300 before Christ by Seleucus Nicator on the lower Orontes. Named for his father Antiochus, the city was meant as capital of his realm, stretched from Mount Silpius to the river, and grew into four walled towns under one rampart. Made a Roman province by Pompey in 64 before Christ, it stayed metropolis of the East, third city of the empire after Rome and Alexandria, with over half a million people.

Seleucids and Romans adorned Antioch with statues, theatres, temples, aqueducts, baths, gardens, and a colonnaded avenue miles long, while the grove of Daphne offered its famed pleasure resort and Apollo temple. Into this great city came the Gospel, and Antioch became a mother church of the East. The entry traces city and church together, from foundation to later centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-classical-lat:
Classical literature, chiefly Latin, shaped Catholic schooling from Roman times onward. When Christianity first appeared in Rome, schooling meant poets and historians, above all Horace and Virgil. New converts carried pagan learning into the Faith, using mythology and rhetoric against paganism. Tertullian forbade Christians to teach, yet allowed pupils to attend school, and his rigour was not followed: Arnobius taught rhetoric, and his pupil Lactantius became professor at Nicomedia.

In the fourth century opposition grew between profane letters and the Bible, hardened by Jerome's psalm translation and by Julian's persecution. Gregory the Great condemned literary study for bishops, Isidore of Seville compressed ancient culture into his Origines, and only Cassiodorus planned a broad union of secular and sacred science. Cluny and Clairvaux reforms later discouraged study, manuscript copying became a secular trade, and in recent times practical men and declared enemies of the Church have attacked Latin training itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commandments-:
John Melody's entry treats the Commandments of the Church under three heads: their nature, their history, and their classification. Lawmaking power over all the faithful belongs to the Church by her very constitution. She holds the deposit of Christian revelation and interprets it for all time. Her universal laws may define doctrine, condemn error, or fix times and manners for keeping divine law. Such laws, binding all the faithful, truly count as commandments of the Church.

History shows the form and number of the precepts shifting across ages and lands. Spanish America kept five, following Aspilcueta in the sixteenth century. French catechisms after Bossuet dropped the last two yet kept Bellarmine's count. The Baltimore council list of 1886 for the United States covers Easter duty, support of pastors, and marriage rules on kindred and forbidden times. Melody thus gives both the theory and the local variety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-ben:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry explains the Communion bench as an adaptation of the sanctuary guard, or altar rail. Before this barrier, in a space called the chancel, the faithful once received Holy Communion standing. Men took the consecrated Bread in their hands. Women received it on a white cloth called the domenical. Deacons gave the Precious Blood, which each person took through a reed of gold or silver.

About the twelfth century, receiving under one kind only became the custom. Priests then laid the small Hosts on communicants' tongues at the rail. Kneeling reception came in about the fifteenth century, and the rail slowly took its modern form. For great crowds, rows of prie-Dieu or benches with Communion cloths and a candle at each row's end may ring the chancel, by decree of the Congregation of Rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-ura:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Urach, Cardinal-Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, born about 1180, died in 1227. Young, he became canon of Saint Lambert's church, Liège cathedral. In 1199 he entered Belgium's Cistercian monastery of Villers, soon becoming prior and in 1209 abbot. In 1214 he was chosen Abbot of Clairvaux, and in 1217 Abbot of Cîteaux and general of his order. Honorius III created him cardinal on 8 January 1219 and charged him with two important legations.

France claimed the first, from 1220 to 1223, to suppress the Albigenses. Germany claimed the second, from 1224 to 1226, to preach and arrange the crusade Frederick II had vowed. After Honorius III died, cardinals agreed to elect Conrad pope, but he refused the dignity. Cistercians venerate him as Blessed, his feast falling on 30 September. A career spanning abbacies, generalship, cardinalate, and refused papacy marks him among the order's leading thirteenth-century figures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-paul-dr:
A biographical entry follows David Paul Drach, a convert from Judaism born at Strasbourg in 1791 and dead at Rome in early 1868. Rosenthal called his conversion one of the century's most important in France. It moved earnest minds to serious study, and drew many fellow Jews toward the Church. Drach's father, a renowned Hebraist and Talmud scholar, gave him his first teaching.

At twelve he entered Talmud school at Edendorf, finishing a three-year course in one year. He then graduated at Bischheim in eighteen months. Teaching at sixteen, he pursued rabbinic learning until his conversion redirected his scholarship. His writings sought to lead fellow Jews to acknowledge Jesus as Messiah. His later work included a great French Bible commentary, with his own contributions on the Pauline and Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diptych:
A diptych is a notebook made of two tablets laid together and joined by rings or a hinge. The tablets were cut from wood, ivory, bone, or metal, and their inner faces were framed and coated with wax. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that Greeks knew such books from the sixth century before Christ. They served as copybooks, for letters, and for many daily uses, and Roman army discharge papers took the same form.

Adding leaves made a triptych or polyptych, and the finest diptychs were richly carved. In church use the diptychs held names read aloud at Mass, the living and the dead. The entry traces that liturgical use to the Memento of the Mass today, where the old reading of names still lives on in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctors-of-th:
Doctors of the Church are writers honored because the whole Church gained from their teaching. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the four great Western fathers of the early Middle Ages, Gregory the Great, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome. Their feasts were ordered as doubles through the whole Church by Boniface the Eighth in 1298. The four became a byword among the schoolmen.

In the East, three doctors stood foremost, John Chrysostom, Basil, and Gregory Nazianzen, whose feasts Leo the Wise made binding through the empire. The entry then follows later additions to the roll and the rules for the honor. It offers a clear guide to a title that marks the Church's most trusted teachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-african:
The Early African Church is the name for the Christian communities of Roman Africa, a coastal strip from Cyrenaica in the east to the river Ampsaga in the west. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds Mauretania, the Atlantic-facing part, and notes that the communities seem to have reached only toward Tangiers. The spread of the faith followed the lines of Roman civilization, starting from Carthage across Proconsular Africa and Numidia, thinning toward Mauretania.

Fixing the church's bounds is hard, since Roman political lines shifted again and again. The entry follows bishops, councils, and writers of a church that gave the West Tertullian, Cyprian, and Augustine. It notes that native Libyan speech lived on only among nomad tribes, while Latin and Punic carried the faith of the cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiasticu:
Ecclesiasticus, also called the Book of Sirach, is the longest of the deuterocanonical books and the last wisdom writing in the Vulgate Old Testament. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its Greek title, the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach. A subscription at the end of newly found Hebrew fragments names the author more fully, Simeon son of Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira.

The full Hebrew heading would read Wisdom of Yeshua son of Sira, though Saint Jerome's prologue complicates the picture. The entry surveys the book's text, versions, and commentators, from Cornely and Konig to Gigot, with studies of the Hebrew fragments by Touzard and Knabenbauer. For readers of the wisdom books, it maps a work long prized and long debated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-henr:
Emmanuel-Henri-Dieudonne Domenech was a French missionary priest and writer, born at Lyons in 1826 and dead in France in 1886. In the spring of 1846, not yet twenty and still short of finishing seminary, he answered an urgent call for missionaries in Texas, then filling fast with American and European settlers. He spent two years at Saint Louis finishing theology and learning English and German.

In May 1848 he was sent to the new German settlement of Castroville, then to Brownsville. The Mexican war had just ended, raiders and outlaws ranged both banks of the Rio Grande, hostile Indians hovered near, and cholera added its horrors. Yet the young priest worked with such energy that he became a power for good across south Texas. His health broke, he returned to France as canon of Montpellier, served as army chaplain in Mexico under Maximilian, and spent his last years in travel and writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephraim-of-an:
Ephraim of Antioch was a defender of the faith of Chalcedon against the Monophysites, born at Amida in Mesopotamia and dead in 545. Under Justinian I he served as Count of the East, and in 527 he succeeded Euphrasius as Patriarch of Antioch. Most of his works are lost, though their titles survive through Anastasius Sinaita, the Sacra Parallela, and Photius.

Anastasius quotes his work against Severus, the Monophysite Patriarch of Antioch from 512 to 519. The Parallela give a passage from his work on John the Grammarian and the synod. Photius describes four books: sermons and letters, a treatise against Severus in three parts, and an answer to five questions on Genesis from a monk, Anatolius. Those fragments are nearly all that remains. Krumbacher holds that, had more survived, Ephraim would rank with Leontius of Byzantium, for his wide knowledge of the Greek Fathers and his following of Cyril of Alexandria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erwin-of-stei:
Erwin of Steinbach was one of the architects of the Strasburg cathedral, date of birth unknown, dead at Strasburg on 17 January 1318. Later tradition calls him Erwin of Steinbach, and Steinbach village near Baden-Baden holds a monument to him. Two of his sons, Erwin and Johannes, his grandson Gerlach from 1341 to 1371, and another scion named Kuntze up to 1382 were also superintending architects.

Hence they were heads of the Strasburg guild of stone-masons, whose influence extended as far as Bavaria, Austria, and the borders of Italy. He must already have proved himself a master-builder elsewhere before taking charge of the Strasburg cathedral façade about 1277. His work on the cathedral shows the influence of the French Gothic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelical-c:
The Evangelical Church in Prussia was the united Protestant church formed in 1817 by King Frederick William III from the Lutheran and Reformed churches. The Reformers had called themselves Evangelicals, followers of the pure Gospel, against Roman tradition. By the early nineteenth century, rationalism and indifference had sapped religious life in Germany, and the king sought one church to match his army, schools, and trade.

On 27 September 1817 he declared his wish to unite the two confessions in his lands into one Evangelical Christian Church, setting the example at Potsdam. Berlin's synod and most clergy answered warmly, and other German states followed, though Saxony, Hanover, and Bavaria held back. The union kept each side's doctrines but gave them one government and one liturgy, the royal Agenda, which met sharp opposition as oppressive and leaning toward Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exarch:
Exarch is a title used in several senses, civil and churchly. In the Roman Empire it meant the governor of a large province. The best known was the Exarch of Italy, who ruled from Ravenna from 552 to 751. In church speech it first meant a metropolitan ruling over other metropolitans.

At Chalcedon in 451 the patriarchs were still called exarchs. Later the name stayed with the metropolitans of Asia, Cappadocia and Pontus, and Thrace. In the East an exarch ranks between patriarch and ordinary metropolitan. Cyprus won the title in 431, Bulgaria took it in 1870, and Georgia's primate bears it still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fathers-of-th:
The Fathers of the Church are the early teachers who handed on apostolic teaching. The name first meant bishops and holy predecessors of each local church. Its limits run from the apostolic age to Gregory the Great in the West. In the East the line reaches John Damascene, who died about 754.

Appeals to the Fathers form one branch of the appeal to tradition. Irenaeus cited the succession of bishops, and Tertullian the agreement of churches. Later teachers like Origen, though priests, shaped doctrine without the title. The article surveys centuries, regions, writings, and schools of patristic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filial-church:
A filial church is a daughter church dependent on an older mother church. Usually it arises when an older parish is divided. Its rector holds a priest's rights but defers in certain accidental matters. He fetches baptismal water and makes a moderate money offering yearly to the mother church.

Some filial churches stand inside an extensive parish without any division. Their pastors act as curates, removable at will by the mother priest. The mother priest may keep baptisms, marriages, and similar offices to himself. In practice curates act as parish priests for their districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-pet:
Francesco Petrarch, born at Arezzo on 20 July 1304 and dead at Arqua on 19 July 1374, was the Italian poet and humanist who helped revive classical learning in Europe. His father, a Florentine court clerk banished with the White Guelphs in 1302, meant him for law, sending him to Montpellier and Bologna. Francesco gave himself to letters, and his father once burned his favourite ancient authors in anger. After his father's death he took minor orders at Avignon, which let him live on church benefices.

There on Good Friday 1327 he first saw Laura, the beloved of his poems. He entered the gay court life of Avignon while building his fame as a Latin scholar and poet. His Italian lyrics, his Latin epic Africa, and his letters shaped the Renaissance idea of the scholar-poet. His search for lost manuscripts of Livy and Cicero made him a founder of humanism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-ittenba:
Franz Ittenbach, born at Konigswinter at the foot of the Drachenfels in 1813 and died at Dusseldorf in 1879, was a German historical painter of deep religion. At nineteen he entered the Dusseldorf Academy, taking private lessons from its president Schadow. With three friends and fellow students, Karl and Andreas Muller and Ernst Deger, he travelled Germany studying and painting. Exceedingly religious, he persistently refused commissions for mythological or pagan subjects and gave his energies almost entirely to church decoration, preparing his greatest works by confession and communion.

His finest paintings stand at Bonn in St. Remigius church and at Breslau in a church of the same saint, with a remarkable Holy Family of 1861 for Prince Liechtenstein's private chapel near Vienna. He also painted many works in Catholic churches across Germany. His sole important fresco was painted in 1844 at Remagen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geography-and:
Geography and the Church argues that the science of the earth's surface owes its greatest debt to Catholic explorers and scholars. Humboldt, Ritter, and Peschel all confessed it. Priests and scholars were once one calling. While greed and conquest pushed discovery, a nobler motive, spreading the faith, sent the bravest, steadiest men into unknown lands through the Middle Ages and beyond.

The survey runs in three parts. First, how church activity opened new lands and peoples in the Middle Ages. Second, what medieval theologians thought of the world. Third, how missionaries and Catholic scholars mapped foreign shores from the age of discovery to the present. Ptolemy's world bounds the start, and Copernicus, himself a churchman, crowns the proof that clerical minds chased the Creator's order in nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-von-pe:
George von Peuerbach, an Austrian astronomer born near Linz in 1423, led Western astronomy based on watching the sky and on maths. Master of arts at Vienna about 1440, he traveled to Italy in 1448, where Bianchini and Cardinal Cusa had him lecture at Ferrara. Refusing Bologna, Padua, and Hungary's court post, he returned to Vienna in 1450 to teach philology and classics. Science he taught chiefly in private.

His most famous pupil was Regiomontanus. Peuerbach reworked Ptolemy's Almagest, replacing chords with sines and tabulating sines for every minute of arc. This was a first step from base-twelve to base-ten counting, done with simple tools like a plumb line. His New Theories of the Planets, first printed at Nuremberg in 1460, joined homocentric spheres with epicycles and grounded school astronomy until years after Copernicus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greek-church:
The Greek Church is a subject treated under terms, the Orthodox Church and its divisions, and the Uniat churches. Its history runs from the first five centuries through the schism and the Crusades to 1453 and the present. A Catholic Encyclopedia article begins by insisting that race, speech, rite, and belief be kept distinct.

Eastern Churches, in the usual sense, means all churches with a rite differing from the Latin. Whether they accept or reject the pope, they cover the Byzantine, Armenian, Syrian, Chaldean, Maronite, and Coptic rites. The Greek Church ordinarily means all churches using the Byzantine Rite, separated or in communion with Rome, whatever their race and speech. Confusion arises precisely when these distinctions are not observed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregor-reisch:
Gregor Reisch was born at Balingen in Wurtemberg about 1467 and died at Freiburg on 9 May 1525. He entered the Carthusian Order after taking his magister at Freiburg in 1489, served as prior at Klein-Basel and then at Freiburg, and visited for the Rhenish province. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar called an oracle.

His chief work, Margarita philosophica of 1503, is an encyclopedia of knowledge in twelve books. It runs from Latin grammar and rhetoric to arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy, physics, natural history, physiology, psychology, and ethics. Cast as questions from the scholar answered by the teacher, with woodcuts and a full index, it became a customary textbook of the higher schools. Alexander von Humboldt said it aided the spread of knowledge for a half-century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heisterbach:
Rhineland Cistercian house Heisterbach in the Siebengebirge began with the hermit Walther on the Petersberg, whose disciples built a monastery in 1134 under Augustine's rule. After Walther's death they moved to Reussrath, and in 1189 Archbishop Philip of Cologne had Himmerod's abbot repeople the empty Petersberg with twelve Cistercians under Abbot Hermann.

Three or four years later the monks moved downhill to Petersthal, called Heisterbach, and raised a basilica begun under Abbot Gerard and consecrated in 1237, blending Romanesque round arches with Gothic points. Rich and flourishing until suppression in 1803, it lost library and archives to Düsseldorf. Church and monastery were sold and torn down in 1809, leaving only its apse and choir ruins, with a monument to its monk Caesarius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henoch:
Henoch, Greek for Enoch, names four biblical figures, of whom the patriarch son of Jared and father of Methuselah is by far the most famous. At sixty-five Henoch fathered Methuselah, and his whole life ran 365 years. Where other patriarchs' sketches close with and he died, his says he walked with God and was taken, seen no more.

Hebrews adds that by faith Henoch was translated not to see death, Sirach agrees. Jude shows him as a prophet announcing God's judgment on the ungodly. Whether Jude quoted the apocryphal Book of Henoch or that book borrowed from Jude is weighed here. The entry favours Jewish tradition as Jude's source and interpolation into the apocryphal book as the likelier path.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-al:
